title: Write a shell script that checks CPU, memory, and disk utilization and alerts if any exceeds a threshold (e.g. 80%).
shortTitle: Shell script that checks CPU, memory, and disk utilization and alerts if any exceeds a threshold
topicTitle: Write a shell script that checks CPU, memory, and disk utilization and alerts if

s1_definition.profdef: A resource-monitoring shell script reads the current CPU, memory, and disk utilization of a host, compares each against a configured threshold such as 80 percent, and raises an alert — logging a warning and optionally sending a notification — whenever any metric crosses its threshold, returning a non-zero exit code so it can gate automation. It is designed to run on a schedule (cron) or as a readiness guard, and it reads values from standard tools so it works on any Linux host without extra agents.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a night-watchman at the National Bank of India who every few minutes checks three gauges — how hard the computers are working (CPU), how full their short-term memory is (RAM), and how full the filing cabinets are (disk). If any gauge goes past the red line at 80 percent, the watchman rings a bell and writes it in the logbook so the on-call engineer can act before the system chokes mid-transaction for Rajesh or Priya.
s1_definition.oneliner: Read CPU, memory, and disk, compare each to the threshold, and alert plus exit non-zero the moment any one crosses it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A resource-monitoring shell script reads the current CPU, memory, and disk utilization of a host, compares each against a configured threshold such as 80 percent, and raises an alert — logging a warning and optionally sending a notification — whenever any metric crosses its threshold, returning a non-zero exit code so it can gate automation. It is designed to run on a schedule (cron) or as a readiness guard, and it reads values from standard tools so it works on any Linux host without extra agents.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a night-watchman at the National Bank of India who every few minutes checks three gauges — how hard the computers are working (CPU), how full their short-term memory is (RAM), and how full the filing cabinets are (disk). If any gauge goes past the red line at 80 percent, the watchman rings a bell and writes it in the logbook so the on-call engineer can act before the system chokes mid-transaction for Rajesh or Priya.

**One line to remember:** Read CPU, memory, and disk, compare each to the threshold, and alert plus exit non-zero the moment any one crosses it.

sections.s2_technical:
The script computes three utilizations. For CPU, a simple and portable approach is to derive busy percentage as 100 minus the idle percentage reported by `top` in batch mode, or to read it from `mpstat` if available; on Linux you can parse `top -bn1`. For memory, you compute used over total from `free`, specifically using the used and total columns so you measure real pressure rather than cached memory. For disk, you read the use percentage of the target filesystem from `df -P`, taking the mount point you care about, usually the root filesystem or the data volume where the database and logs live.

Each metric is compared against a threshold, defaulting to 80 but overridable through an environment variable or argument, so the same script serves different hosts with different sensitivities. When a metric crosses the threshold, the script logs a timestamped warning line with the metric name and value, appends it to a log file for audit, and optionally sends a notification — for example posting to a webhook or sending mail — so the on-call engineer is paged. Keeping the alert channel pluggable means the same core works whether you use Slack, PagerDuty, or email.

The script sets the exit code based on whether any threshold was breached: zero when everything is healthy and non-zero when at least one metric is over, which lets it act as a gate in automation — a deployment pipeline or a health probe can fail fast if the host is already saturated. Good practice includes `set -euo pipefail` so the script fails loudly on errors and does not silently continue after a failed command, quoting all variable expansions to avoid word-splitting, validating that the required tools exist before using them, and using integer comparison carefully by stripping the percent sign and decimal part. For banking operations you also make the thresholds and the monitored filesystem configurable, log in a consistent machine-parseable format so a log shipper can index the alerts, and keep the script idempotent and side-effect free apart from logging and alerting, so running it on a tight cron schedule is safe.
sections.s3_banking:
A National Bank of India transaction host must never silently run out of CPU, memory, or disk during business hours, because a saturated host drops transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya. We want a small, dependable shell script, scheduled by cron, that checks all three and alerts the moment any crosses 80 percent.

Problem 1 — If disk fills up, the database cannot write and transactions fail. The script checks disk use percent on the data volume and alerts early so the team adds space before it is full.

Problem 2 — If memory is exhausted, the JVM running the transfer service is OOM-killed mid-transaction. The script checks memory pressure and warns before it reaches that point.

Problem 3 — If CPU is pinned, every request slows and timeouts cascade. The script checks CPU busy percent and alerts so the team can scale out. The script is self-contained, uses only standard tools, logs every alert with a timestamp, and exits non-zero on any breach so it can gate automation.

sections.s4d_java:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ─── File: bin/check_resources.sh ───
# National Bank of India — host resource monitor.
# Checks CPU, memory, disk; alerts + exits non-zero if any exceeds threshold.

set -euo pipefail

# ---- Configuration (override via env or etc/monitor.env) ----
THRESHOLD="${THRESHOLD:-80}"                 # percent
MOUNT="${MOUNT:-/}"                          # filesystem to check
LOG_FILE="${LOG_FILE:-logs/resource-alerts.log}"
WEBHOOK_URL="${WEBHOOK_URL:-}"               # optional Slack/Teams webhook

mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LOG_FILE")"

# ---- Helper: timestamped log line ----
log() {
    # $1 = level, $2 = message
    local ts
    ts="$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')"
    printf '%s [%-7s] %s\n' "$ts" "$1" "$2" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
}

# ---- Helper: send alert to webhook if configured ----
send_alert() {
    local msg="$1"
    log "WARNING" "$msg"
    if [[ -n "$WEBHOOK_URL" ]]; then
        curl -fsS -X POST "$WEBHOOK_URL" \
             -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
             -d "{\"text\":\"NBI host alert: ${msg}\"}" >/dev/null || \
             log "SEVERE" "Failed to post alert to webhook"
    fi
}

# ---- Verify required tools exist ----
for tool in top free df awk; do
    command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { log "SEVERE" "Missing tool: $tool"; exit 2; }
done

breached=0   # becomes 1 if any metric exceeds threshold

# ---- CPU: busy% = 100 - idle% (from top batch mode) ----
cpu_idle="$(top -bn1 | awk -F'[,%]' '/Cpu\(s\)/ {for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /id/){gsub(/[^0-9.]/,"",$(i-1)); print $(i-1)}}')"
cpu_busy="$(awk -v idle="${cpu_idle:-0}" 'BEGIN{printf "%d", 100 - idle}')"
if (( cpu_busy >= THRESHOLD )); then
    send_alert "CPU ${cpu_busy}% >= ${THRESHOLD}% threshold"
    breached=1
else
    log "INFO" "CPU ${cpu_busy}% (ok)"
fi

# ---- Memory: used/total * 100 (from free) ----
mem_used_pct="$(free | awk '/^Mem:/ {printf "%d", $3/$2 * 100}')"
if (( mem_used_pct >= THRESHOLD )); then
    send_alert "Memory ${mem_used_pct}% >= ${THRESHOLD}% threshold"
    breached=1
else
    log "INFO" "Memory ${mem_used_pct}% (ok)"
fi

# ---- Disk: use% of target filesystem (from df) ----
disk_used_pct="$(df -P "$MOUNT" | awk 'NR==2 {gsub(/%/,"",$5); print $5}')"
if (( disk_used_pct >= THRESHOLD )); then
    send_alert "Disk ${disk_used_pct}% on ${MOUNT} >= ${THRESHOLD}% threshold"
    breached=1
else
    log "INFO" "Disk ${disk_used_pct}% on ${MOUNT} (ok)"
fi

if (( breached == 1 )); then
    log "SEVERE" "One or more resources exceeded ${THRESHOLD}% — paging on-call"
    exit 1
fi
log "INFO" "All resources healthy (CPU/mem/disk < ${THRESHOLD}%)"
exit 0
```

```bash
# ─── File: etc/monitor.env ───
# Source this before running, or export in the cron entry.
export THRESHOLD=80
export MOUNT=/data                       # the banking data volume
export LOG_FILE=/var/log/nbi/resource-alerts.log
export WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXXX/YYYY/ZZZZ
```

```bash
# ─── File: cron/nbi-monitor.cron ───
# Run every 5 minutes; load config first.
*/5 * * * * . /opt/nbi/etc/monitor.env && /opt/nbi/bin/check_resources.sh
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Make executable
chmod +x bin/check_resources.sh

# Run once with defaults (threshold 80, mount /)
./bin/check_resources.sh

# Run with a custom threshold and data volume
THRESHOLD=75 MOUNT=/data ./bin/check_resources.sh

# Check exit code (0 = healthy, 1 = breach, 2 = missing tool)
echo "exit=$?"

# Install the cron schedule
crontab cron/nbi-monitor.cron
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the script runs on an NBI transaction host with threshold 80 and the data volume mounted at /data.

Step 1 — The script loads configuration: threshold 80, mount /data, the log file path, and an optional webhook. It verifies the required tools (top, free, df, awk) exist, exiting with code 2 if any is missing.

Step 2 — It computes CPU busy percent as 100 minus the idle percent from `top`. Suppose idle is 12 percent, so busy is 88 percent, which is at or above 80, so it sends a warning alert and sets the breached flag.

Step 3 — It computes memory used percent from `free` as used over total. Suppose that is 64 percent, which is under 80, so it logs an informational healthy line.

Step 4 — It reads disk use percent of /data from `df`. Suppose that is 91 percent, which is at or above 80, so it sends a disk warning alert and keeps the breached flag set.

Step 5 — Because at least one metric breached, the script logs a severe line stating resources exceeded the threshold and pages on-call, then exits with code 1, which lets any pipeline or probe calling it fail fast.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 02:20:00 [INFO   ] CPU 88% ... 
2026-10-30 02:20:00 [WARNING] CPU 88% >= 80% threshold
2026-10-30 02:20:00 [INFO   ] Memory 64% (ok)
2026-10-30 02:20:00 [WARNING] Disk 91% on /data >= 80% threshold
2026-10-30 02:20:00 [SEVERE ] One or more resources exceeded 80% — paging on-call
# exit code: 1
```

```
  ┌─ Design Principles Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ check_resources.sh           │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ log(level, msg)              │  timestamped, tee to LOG_FILE
  │ send_alert(msg)              │  log WARNING + optional webhook
  │ [preflight] tool check       │  exit 2 if missing
  │ [CPU block]  busy=100-idle   │  breached=1 if ≥ THRESHOLD
  │ [MEM block]  used/total      │  breached=1 if ≥ THRESHOLD
  │ [DISK block] df %            │  breached=1 if ≥ THRESHOLD
  │ [verdict] breached? exit 1:0 │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: One Run ────────────────────────────────────────

  [START] → [TOOLS_OK] → [CPU_CHECKED] → [MEM_CHECKED] → [DISK_CHECKED]
      │                                                        │
      │ missing tool                                           ▼
      ▼                                                 breached?
  [EXIT 2]                                       ┌──────┴───────┐
                                                 ▼              ▼
                                            [EXIT 1 alert]  [EXIT 0 healthy]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. cron → check_resources.sh
  2.   → preflight tool check
  3.   → CPU: top → compute busy → compare → maybe send_alert()
  4.   → MEM: free → compute used% → compare → maybe send_alert()
  5.   → DISK: df → use% → compare → maybe send_alert()
  6.   → verdict: exit 1 (breach) or exit 0 (healthy)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I write the resource-monitoring script to read three utilizations and compare each against a configurable threshold, defaulting to 80 percent, and to alert and exit non-zero the moment any one crosses it. For CPU I derive busy percent as 100 minus the idle percent reported by top in batch mode; for memory I compute used over total from free so I measure real pressure rather than cached memory; and for disk I read the use percent of the data volume from df. Each metric is compared against the threshold, and when one is breached I write a timestamped warning line to an append-only log for audit and optionally post to a webhook so the on-call engineer is paged.

The script is written defensively because it runs unattended on a tight cron schedule. I use set with errexit, nounset, and pipefail so it fails loudly instead of silently continuing after a failed command, I quote every variable expansion to avoid word-splitting, and I verify that the required tools exist before using them, exiting with a distinct code if any is missing. The threshold and the monitored filesystem are configurable through environment variables so the same script serves different hosts, and the alert channel is pluggable so it works with Slack, PagerDuty, or email without changing the core logic. Crucially, the exit code reflects health — zero when everything is fine and non-zero on any breach — so the script can also act as a gate in a deployment pipeline or a readiness probe that fails fast when a host is already saturated.

In my project at the National Bank of India this script runs every five minutes on each transaction host, because a host that silently runs out of CPU, memory, or disk drops transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya. When disk on the data volume crossed 80 percent it alerted early so the team added space before the database could no longer write, and when memory climbed it warned before the transfer service JVM would be OOM-killed mid-transaction. The principle I always state is to keep the script simple, portable, and side-effect free apart from logging and alerting, make thresholds and channels configurable, and return a meaningful exit code so it is useful both as a scheduled alarm and as an automation guard.
